prompt:
Write an essay of about 800 words on the subject below.

Write it the way an excellent, idiosyncratic human essayist would: someone with real expertise and strong opinions, writing in the first person for their own blog. Commit to a specific thesis that a thoughtful reader might disagree with. Use concrete particulars (names, numbers, incidents, things only someone who had done the work would know) in place of general statements. Vary sentence length. No headings, no bullet points, no summary paragraph at the end, and none of the stock phrases of AI writing.

Output only the essay, with no title.

Subject: an essay on whether it is wrong to eat animals
raw:
For three summers I killed chickens on a small farm in the Hudson Valley, about a hundred and twenty birds every other Saturday. You carry them upside down by the legs, which quiets them, and lower each one headfirst into a galvanized cone so the head pokes out the bottom. One cut under the jaw on each side. Then ninety seconds of bleeding, a dunk in water held at 148 degrees, and half a minute in a drum plucker lined with rubber fingers. People assume the killing is what complicated meat for me. The killing was the part I could defend.

What I couldn't defend was the bird. We raised Cornish Cross, close kin to the Cobb 500 and Ross 308 that fill commercial barns, because that is what customers will pay for: a wide breast on a four-and-a-half-pound carcass in seven weeks. In 1950 a broiler needed about ten weeks to reach three pounds. By week six ours would walk four steps across good pasture and sit down. They ate lying at the feeder. If we got busy and let a batch run to week ten, we'd find a few dead each morning, on their backs, bellies full of fluid, hearts given out. These were the lucky ones, on grass and moved daily, sold at $7 a pound to people who wanted to feel fine about dinner. The suffering was bred into them, and no amount of pasture fixes a skeleton that can't carry its own meat.

So here is my position, which annoys my vegan friends and my hunting friends about equally. It is not wrong to eat an animal. It is wrong to eat nearly all the animals actually on offer, and the conventional ranking of sins is upside down. The steak is the most defensible thing in the butcher's case. The chicken breast and the egg are the worst.

Do the arithmetic. A steer yields roughly 450 pounds of retail meat; a broiler, about four. That's one death against a hundred-odd, and the steer, even one finished in a feedlot, spent its first six or eight months beside its mother on grass, in a body that works. The United States slaughters around nine billion chickens a year and about thirty-three million cattle. When a well-meaning person swaps beef for chicken, on a cardiologist's advice or for the climate, he multiplies the number of animals he answers for by a hundred and moves every one of them from a mediocre life to a bad one. Eggs are no refuge. A modern hen lays about three hundred a year from a frame whose jungle-fowl ancestor laid perhaps a dozen, and she strips calcium out of her own bones to shell them. Her brothers were macerated on their first day because a layer-breed cockerel is worth nothing to anyone. The word "vegetarian" covers a great deal of that.

Why isn't the killing itself the wrong? Because every animal dies, and almost none die well. A wild turkey gets a coyote, or starvation in February. A ewe on the best farm in Vermont eventually gets a captive bolt, which is faster than anything nature has ever arranged. I think what we owe an animal is a life worth having and a death without terror, and I think that debt can be paid in full. Peter Singer, whom everyone cites and few reread, built *Animal Liberation* on suffering, not on a right to life. Tom Regan went the other way and said a creature that is the subject of a life cannot be used at all. I've read Regan twice and I still can't make the argument hold for a mussel, or explain why the fox is innocent and I'm not.

The objection that actually lands is practical. Something like 99 percent of American farm animals live in confinement, so my careful distinction applies to a rounding error, and "I only eat humane meat" is usually a story told over a restaurant plate of unknown origin. The law won't rescue you either: the Humane Methods of Slaughter Act of 1958 does not cover poultry at all. So the honest version of my view is nearly as austere as veganism. It just draws the line somewhere else.

I buy a quarter of a steer each October from a man two roads over, about 110 pounds of beef wrapped in white paper, and it lasts the year. I eat mussels and oysters without a flicker, since there's nobody home. I haven't bought chicken since 2016. Eggs only from hens I've stood next to.

In my last summer I tried to talk the farm's owner into switching to Freedom Rangers, a slower bird that takes eleven or twelve weeks and can still run at the end of it. He penciled it out on the back of a feed receipt: $11 a pound to break even. He slid the receipt across the table and asked me how many of our Saturday customers I thought would pay that. I said maybe ten. He said four.
